What's new in the World Development Indicators, October 2026: poverty and inequality updates, new food security & nutrition data, latest energy statistics

World Bank Data Team

October 22, 2026

This page in:

English

English

On October 8, 2026, the World Development Indicators (WDI) database published new and revised data across a wide range of development topics. 
 
What’s New in the October 2026 Release? 
People

Food security and nutrition data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) now run through 2024, including the prevalence of undernourishment and of moderate or severe food insecurity. 

Labor market indicators have also been refreshed with the latest national estimates from the International Labour Organization (ILO): employment-to-population ratios, labor force participation, unemployment, youth not in employment, education or training (NEET), part-time employment, and the share of women in senior and middle management, broken down by age and sex where available.
 

Prosperity

Poverty and inequality indicators are updated through 2025. They cover headcount ratios and poverty gaps at the $3.00, $4.20, and $8.30 a day poverty lines (2021 PPP); societal, national, and multidimensional poverty; the Gini index and income shares; and shared prosperity indicators tracking income growth among the bottom 40 percent.

The Worldwide Governance Indicators now include estimates and scores through 2025 for all six dimensions, from Control of Corruption to Voice and Accountability. 

Balance of payments indicators have been refreshed with the latest IMF data, including foreign direct investment inflows, remittances as a share of GDP, current account balances, and exports of goods and services. 

Purchasing power parity (PPP) conversion factor for households and NPISHs final consumption expenditure is updated using Consumer Price Index (CPI) data sourced from IMF

Data on military expenditure and arms transfers are now available for 2025.
 

Planet

New 2024 data have been published on access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking (used to monitor SDG 7.1.2) for total, urban, and rural populations.

Access to clean cooking has expanded steadily. By 2024, 75 percent of people worldwide had access to clean fuels and technologies for cooking. The remaining challenge is increasingly concentrated outside cities.Progress has been uneven. In 2024, access had reached around 90 percent in urban areas, compared with just 56 percent in rural communities.Regional trajectories vary widely. The access level in Sub-Saharan Africa remains much below that of other regions.South Asia and East Asia & Pacific have made especially rapid gains. In South Asia, rural access increased from 6 percent in 2000 to 62 percent in 2024, sharply narrowing the divide with cities. The East Asia & Pacific region has also made rapid progress.Regional averages mask substantial differences in access and speed of change. For example, both Indonesia and Viet Nam increased rural access by 82 percentage points in the span of 24 years.Select a country to see how access has changed in urban and rural areas, and whether the gap is narrowing, persisting, or widening.

 

Energy statistics from the International Energy Agency (IEA) have been refreshed with 2024 data for non-OECD economies and, for selected electricity indicators, 2025 data for OECD economies. 

New 2024 FAO data cover fertilizer use, land use, forests, irrigation, and cereal production and yields, together with updated crop, livestock, and food production indexes.
 

Infrastructure

Data from the World Intellectual Property Organization on patent, industrial design, and trademark applications by residents and non-residents have been updated for 2022–2024.

 
Where to find it
As always, the data is available through the Open Data site, DataBank, the Data Catalog, bulk downloads, and the WDI API. The full details are in the October 2026 release note.
